back: Immunity from the body's own immune response; memory cells formed; slow to develop, long-lasting.
Immunity from received antibodies; no memory cells; immediate but short-lived.

front: Examples of the four types of immunity
back: Natural active: infection. Artificial active: vaccine. Natural passive: placenta, breast milk. Artificial passive: antitoxin, antivenom.
Live attenuated (measles, BCG), inactivated, subunit (hepatitis B, HPV), toxoid (tetanus).

front: How does a vaccine give protection?
back: Antigens cause a primary response and memory cells; real infection meets a fast secondary response.
Enough of a population is immune that the pathogen cannot spread, protecting the unvaccinated.
Stable antigens, no animal reservoir, visible cases, no carriers, heat-stable live vaccine, ring vaccination.

front: Why is antigenic variation a problem?
back: Memory cells made against old antigens do not recognise new ones (influenza, HIV, malaria).
Keeping vaccines at about 2-8 °C from manufacture to use so antigens are not denatured.
